title: Stepping Stone Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Stepping Stone wells have a 360 ft median depth; see yields, water levels, drilling costs, and local risks before buying.
h1: Stepping Stone, Colorado Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Stepping Stone means understanding the well beneath it, not just the house above it. Records within 5 miles show a wide range of depths, strong reported yields, and substantial variation in static water levels. The area includes Meridian Village, Sierra Ridge, Stonegate, Grand View Estates, Parker, and Meridian.

These figures come from Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records. They describe nearby permitted wells, not a guarantee for a particular lot. A neighboring well can still be the best starting point for a driller, especially where fractured bedrock or changing sedimentary layers affect the result.

sections.heading: Stepping Stone well depths reflect Denver Basin geology
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Stepping Stone is 360 feet. The middle half runs from 190 to 540 feet, meaning a bid based only on a shallow neighbor could be misleading. About 42% of wells fall between 300 and 600 feet, while 19% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 3,220 feet.

Depths vary because permits identify both Denver Basin aquifers and unnamed or fractured-bedrock sources. Lower Dawson appears on 1,106 permits, Denver on 435, and 1,682 name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. For a drilling estimate, use the local depth range rather than treating the median as a promised depth.

sections.heading: Reported well yields are generally useful, but verify the test
sections.html:
Reported pump yields are comparatively strong in this area. The median is 13.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 11.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. About 58% of reporting wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 41% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No recorded reporting wells fall below 5 gallons per minute.

That is encouraging for a household, but it is not a guarantee of storage, pressure, or long-term performance. Only 1,266 wells report a pump yield, compared with 2,114 recorded as constructed. Ask for the well completion report and pumping-test details, then have the system checked for tank size, pump capacity, and water quality.

sections.heading: Water levels vary widely rather than showing a simple decline
sections.html:
The median static water level is 278 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 100 to 480 feet. That range matters when estimating pump depth, electrical needs, and the work required to bring water into a proposed home. Only 184 records report a static water level, so the data is much thinner than the depth and permit record.

The decade figures do not establish a steady downward trend. Median depth to water was 123 feet in the 1970s, 236 in the 1980s, 702 in the 2000s, 382 in the 2010s, and 161 in the 2020s. Different wells, locations, and measurement conditions likely drive much of that spread. Use a nearby, comparable well rather than the decade series alone.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long-term drilling around Stepping Stone
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 4,361 permitted wells within the study area, though only part of that group reports construction details. Permit activity was highest in the 1980s, with 853 permits, after 756 in the 1970s. The record includes 253 permits from the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequently listed drillers are Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.) with 641 records, Hier Drilling Co. (Hier, Peter J) with 440, and Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 373. Old permits are useful for patterns, but a current driller should still review the exact parcel, access, setbacks, and intended use.

sections.heading: A median-depth Stepping Stone well costs real money
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 360-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $18,000 to $25,200. That is drilling only, not the complete water system.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $24,000 to $37,200 at the median depth. A deeper-than-average hole can move beyond that range, while difficult access or additional site work can affect the final bid. Get the drilling allowance, casing and grout assumptions, pump equipment, testing, and connection work listed separately.

sections.heading: Check water quality, dry-hole exposure, and building constraints
sections.html:
Yield is only one part of the risk. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 98 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 11 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove a problem on a particular property, but they are a reason to test existing well water and review environmental records before closing.

Confirm the well permit allows the intended household, stock, or irrigation use. Domestic and household wells make up 54% of the use mix; stock is 12% and irrigation is 6%. Check septic setbacks, reserve areas, driveway access, utility routing, and the building envelope before drilling. A dry hole or low-producing well can leave you with a difficult site plan and a large sunk cost.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Stepping Stone, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Stepping Stone is 360 feet. The middle half runs from 190 to 540 feet, and 19% of wells are deeper than 600 feet. About 42% fall between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest record is 3,220 feet, showing why a parcel-specific estimate matters.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Stepping Stone?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 360-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $18,000 to $25,200. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $24,000 to $37,200. Access, depth, and final equipment can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Stepping Stone?
faq.a: Among nearby records reporting pump yield, the median is 13.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 11.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 58% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 41% report more than 15. Confirm performance with the completion report and a current inspection.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Stepping Stone?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from yield or depth alone. Within about 10 miles, records show 98 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 11 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property’s water for relevant contaminants and review nearby environmental records before relying on the well.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Stepping Stone?
faq.a: The available records do not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was 123 feet in the 1970s, 236 in the 1980s, 702 in the 2000s, 382 in the 2010s, and 161 in the 2020s. Only 184 wells report static water levels, so these figures should be treated as variable local measurements, not a basin-wide trend.
